Mr. Speaker, I am advised as follows. The R.C.M.P. arrested Charles Wilson pursuant to section 16 of the Immigration Act. This section does not require a warrant for arrest of a person who, there are reasonable grounds to believe, came into Canada by reason of false or misleading information or other fraudulent or improper means.
Certain articles and money were taken into the possession of the R.C.M.P. with the consent of Mr. Wilson. All moneys and articles taken into the possession of the R.C.M.P. were later given back to Mr. Wilson, and a receipt was obtained for them. January 31, 1968

Canada, will the minister, in conjunction with the Department of Trade and Commerce, be announcing the development of a comprehensive sugar policy for Canada which will permit the continuation of this part of the agricultural industry in Canada?

maintopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON NATIONAL POLICY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have seen the officials of the company which is closing its plant in the Chatham area, and I intend to see the producers concerning the effect on their livelihood of the closing of the plant and the possibility of diverting to other crops. subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY OF CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Is the Prime Minister in a position to tell the house whether the Canadian members of the international control commission in Viet Nam have been in any danger or have suffered any casualties as a result of the street fighting in Saigon?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have received a preliminary report from our delegation in Saigon which indicates that to the best of the delegation's knowledge there have been no casualties among Canadians serving with the delegation.
However, in the disturbed conditions now prevailing it may take a little time to obtain formal confirmation of this from those Canadians who are serving at commission posts outside Saigon, and also from Canadians living and working in South Viet Nam in capacities other than commission assignments. We are making inquiries as to the position of those Canadians outside Saigon, and as soon as we receive some information I will make it available to the house.

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY OF CANADIANS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I was wondering whether the government was considering advising those Canadians who are not in Viet Nam on official duty as members of the international control commission, but who are on other duties that are perhaps of a non-governmental nature, to leave the country under the present circumstances.

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY OF CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the members of the commission do have information about Canadians working outside the commission. The commission is trying to get in touch with them, and if there are developments that would require them to leave their official duties, or their duties whatever they may be, and come back to Canada I am sure

they will be given that advice. However, I hope to have a report on all this shortly, and I will be able to give more information at that time.

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY OF CANADIANS
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the right hon. gentleman whether the report of the Canadian envoy who went to Hanoi as a result of the peace feelers has yet been received and, if so, what it indicates?

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-INQUIRY AS TO SAFETY OF CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the only report I have received is from our representative who is in Hanoi. It indicates that he has had discussions there, that he will be returning to Saigon very shortly-indeed, he may have reached Saigon within the last day or so-and that when he does return to Saigon he will be in a position to send a report on his mission. That report I have not yet seen. Whether it has come in during the day I am not sure, but I will make inquiries.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps it is true that the word "paramount" is the one that gives most trouble to members of the committee. I have checked with the dictionary which I obtained from the table, which says that "paramount" can mean either "supreme" or "superior". I suggest that read in the light of the whole sentence, the amendment does not put the public system invariably in the position of winning that particular battle, but rather it is the public interest that must be considered; and those who will have to judge that question are to be the council. They will have to give paramount consideration, or superior consideration, to the objectives of the national broadcasting system. I think that the word "paramount" has, in the eyes of the law, acquired precision by interpretation and I do not think it bears the interpretation that my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre suggests.
To me it is not a matter of supremacy but one of superiority. I have looked at the definitions in the "supremacy" and "superiority" fields. "Supreme", for example, means "the

greatest possible", "uttermost", "extreme", "last and greatest" or "most important". I think all those definitions show some limitation, and suggest that "paramount" would not invariably, or 100 per cent, throw the decision in any conflict in favour of, say, the C.B.C. as opposed to private interests.
After all, the first thing the council must consider in its decision in any conflict is the public interest. They must say: We have one guide line, namely that the people of Canada, through the C.B.C., are spending a great deal of money on the public service. speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of immediately introducing legislation to provide the following increase of the compensation paid for the cattle slaughtered under the authority of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act:	(a) purebred
cattle, $200 (b) crossbred cattle, $125.

He said: Mr. Speaker, on May 9 last I was privileged to put on the order paper the notice of motion which you have just read and which I should like to quote again:
In the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of immediately introducing legislation to provide the following increase of the compensation paid for the cattle slaughtered under the authority of the Animal Contagious Disease Act: (a) purebred cattle, $200.00 (b) crossbred cattle, $125.00.
Mr. Speaker, I decided to put the motion I have just read on the order paper following conversations which I had with farmers and stock-breeders in my region. They put pressure on me and made representations urging me to take this position.
Agriculture
I have the honour of representing here a riding where stock-breeding is a major industry. The region of Saint-Hyacinthe is renowned for its purebred livestock. The interested farmers in Saint-Hyacinthe itself to to a great deal of trouble in order to improve their livestock. As you know, for instance the former dairy school is now in the Institute of Agricultural Technology. There is also a veterinary school and, near the institute, there is the artificial insemination centre.
During the years when the artificial insemination centre was in operation, the farmers of my region made good use of the facilities provided by the government of the province. As a result, the herds of all the farmers and particularly of livestock breeders have improved considerably.
Anyone who had the opportunity to viEit the Saint-Hyacinthe exhibition, for instance, where six or seven surrounding counties as well as the Rougemont county are represented, comes to the conclusion that the farmers in the Richelieu area are quite prosperous and eager to have first grade cattle.
Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, that such improvement is not possible without significant expenses on the part of the farmers concerned and, from one year to the next, the operating cost of a farm rises.
The Animal Contagious Diseases Act was implemented a few years ago and amendments to increase the compensation paid for the cattle slaughtered in case of contagious disease have been brought in. It was in August 1958 that such compensations were increased for the last time; previously, the compensation paid for a slaughtered purebred animal was $100, and it was raised to $140. On the other hand, the compensation paid for a cross-bred animal, which was $40, was raised to $70.
The aim of that motion is not to grant a subsidy to farmers whose animals are struck by a contagious disease. It is recognized that, in some cases, the present indemnity covers quite well the losses incurred but, in cases where the meat cannot be eaten, it is also recognized that the present indemnity is much lower than the loss incurred.
For those reasons the members of the Catholic Farmers Union I met as well as members of other farm organizations in my riding have asked me to make representations to the government to improve further the situation, so that a breeder whose herd is struck by an infectious disease will not lose too much.

January 31, 1968
Agriculture
If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) really wants the farmers not to suffer in cases such as those I have just mentioned, he will surely have that motion passed at once, so that the farmers will not be liable to sometimes irretrievable losses.
We merely have to recall, for instance, the epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease we had in 1948, if I remember well, to realize how fast a farmer, a breeder, can be let to the brink of ruin.
There is always a possibility of such epidemics invading our land, so much so that the department takes proper steps by placing animals imported into our country in quarantine. It is only fair and reasonable for the government to take such measures for the protection of our animals' health. But it is also reasonable, I think, to put forward the views of Canadian farmers and livestock breeders and claim fair protection for them.
To prevent the Minister of Agriculture from saying: We are well disposed, but you did not give us time to take action, I immediately end my remarks and give the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Beer) the opportunity to take part in the debate and make recommendations allowing this motion I just moved to become an accomplished fact. I should like to ask him to act in such a way that we will be called upon to vote before the private members' hour is over.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASED COMPENSATION FOR SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
I have listened with considerable interest to the motion presented by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) and the tribute he has paid to the livestock breeders in his constituency. I am well aware of the high quality of the livestock produced in that area. I think it is constituencies such as his which have contributed to the great name Canada enjoys throughout the world for outstanding livestock. He has suggested also he is quite confident it would be the wish of the Canadian Department of Agriculture to provide reasonable protection in the event of loss.
The resolution moved by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot states that, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of immediately introducing legislation to provide for an increase in the compensation paid for cattle slaughtered under the authority of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.

This act is designed to prevent the introduction or spread of serious animal diseases in Canada and to prevent the export of diseased livestock or livestock products, thus maintaining the excellent record this country enjoys throughout the world for healthy, disease free livestock. In its animal disease control and eradication program, the department has for many years provided compensation to owners whose animals have been ordered destroyed. There are two broad headings under which this compensation is paid. One case deals with cattle ordered slaughtered under an area or herd eradication program, such as tuberculosis and brucellosis. The other is where the department is dealing with a more serious contagious disease such as an outbreak of hog cholera in swine or the outbreak of foot and mouth disease such as occurred in 1952.
Under the area of herd eradication program, officers of the department conduct testing programs for cattle diseases such as tuberculosis and brucellosis. Any infected animals are destroyed and compensation paid to the owners to provide assistance in replacing the diseased animals with disease free stock, thus improving their herds. During the last fiscal year compensation paid to owners who had animals destroyed totalled almost $1 million.
Under these programs for the eradication of tuberculosis and brucellosis, it should be pointed out that any animals required to be slaughtered under the provisions of the act which are infected with tuberculosis and brucellosis, are a potential source of loss to the owner even if those programs were not carried out. The owner therefore does benefit materially and directly by the removal of a diseased animal from his herd, since it is not only a danger to the health of the rest of the herd but also reduces his potential returns from his production. On the other hand, it is also in the national interest from the consumer's point of view that our livestock products should come from healthy animals.
Under the area of herd eradication program, the present rates of compensation are $140 purebred and $70 for grade animals. Here, we are dealing with individual animals, not the destruction of an entire herd. In another example where an entire herd is to be destroyed, compensation is paid to the owner at market value. In this case, which is somewhat different from the case involving brucellosis and tuberculosis, not only the infected but all exposed and contact animals are ordered destroyed. This action is taken as
January 31, 1968

a measure to protect the total livestock industry and to prevent the spread of the disease throughout the country. It follows, then, that the owner of such a herd is compensated at full value.
It should not be overlooked in the case of tuberculosis or brucellosis that in addition to the compensation awarded by the department, the owner also receives the meat or carcass salvage value from the packaging establishment where the animals are slaughtered. Therefore an owner's compensation returns, made up of the department's compensation plus the meat salvage value, go a long way toward assisting the owner in obtaining disease free animals.
Should the reactor animal be condemned at the time of slaughter as unfit for food, the department pays the owner the equivalent of the meat salvage carcass value so that in any case the owner's returns are the same. Notwithstanding this, we have been concerned about actual compensation values being paid owners, particularly the existing relationship between the compensation an owner now receives from the department and the actual market value of the animal. Consideration is now being given to a review of the compensation paid for animals slaughtered under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.

January 31, 1968
Agriculture
I am speaking of this from personal knowledge, because when I was with the C.F.U., I often had to prepare statements and try to balance the budget of farmers whose herd had suffered from this terrible sickness which is brucellosis. Let me say in passing that losses due to tuberculosis are covered by the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, and it is almost checked in Canada. Furthermore brucellosis is also being checked. Considerable efforts have been made by the government in this direction since nearly 4.5 per cent of the cattle in Canada was affected by brucellosis in 1957 and this percentage has been brought down to 1.5 per cent in 1967. This makes us realize that the situation has greatly improved.
On the other hand, while this percentage was decreasing, the value of the cattle increased threefold. In 1957 the farmers were receiving a sum of $70 when they had to destroy cattle worth $150 to $175. Today the same cattle has increased in value by $250, $300, even $350 but the compensation has remained at the same point.
So, I think it is normal that this compensation should be increased to $200 and to $125. Even if we were to be more generous, if the minister agreed or if his estimates allowed a compensation of $125 for cross-bred cattle, we would be more generous than the C.F.U. requests.
This year, I attended the congress of the C.F.U. and I examined with the utmost interest the demands that were made to increase compensation to $100 for cross-bred cattle and to $200 for pure-bred cattle. This was being asked by Quebec Farmers Association. But I think that in asking $125 the member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot is possibly more generous and I support him, because if the farmers are asking only $100, it is because they are not used to receiving considerable compensation and that they cannot have the act amended.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) is fully aware of the problem and I can tell the member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot that I have discussed this with the minister. I have shown him that the problem is important, because I have met the leaders of the C.F.U. of my area and those of the St. Hyacinthe area. These leaders are colleagues of mine and, furthermore, they are people with whom I have worked on the social level. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of the motion of my colleague. Stockmen have long been aware that the present compensation for slaughtered animals is inadequate. In view of rising costs and values it is no longer realistic at this time.
I do not wish to question the terminology of the motion, but I should like to refer to purebred cattle as registered cattle. When applying for compensation for purebred animals one must produce their registered papers in order to prove they are purebred.
There are many t.b., Bangs, or brucellosis-free areas in Canada today. In fact, in many areas there have been very few reactors in use of late. The calfhood vaccination program against brucellosis protects animals against this disease, and because these diseases have to a great extent been eliminated there is not much danger of the cost of compensation to the government being as great as it once was.
There are dangers in compensation that is too small, and some of these have shown up in the hesitancy of some owners to report suspicious cases of disease in time to check its spread. In other words, there is the tendency on the part of some owners not to co-operate with the authorities because they know that if certain of their animals are condemned they will get little return for them. An example of this, Mr. Speaker, is the purchase of a registered animal at a very high price. The animal would have been tested before sale for both t.b. and brucellosis, but the new owner is rather nervous about having the animal retested in case there is a reaction. And you cannot blame him. Therefore I think there is great need for a more realistic compensation figure when an animal or a group of animals is condemned.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) for bringing forward this resolution. Although there has not been too much time for research, it is certainly overdue. I went back over the history of compensation from 1952. In that year the compensation paid under the act for purebred cattle was limited to $100 and for grade cattle to $40. The same figures applied, with some change in the

method of payment, in 1953-54. In the amendments introduced in 1958, the government of the day saw fit to increase the compensation for thoroughbred cattle to $140 and for grade cattle to $70.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I looked up the report of the livestock market in Toronto for yesterday and found that these prices are quite out of line with present day cattle prices. The hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Moore) has mentioned cows and high priced breeding animals in the dairy end of the business. I suggest to the parliamentary secretary who, I notice, is now in his seat, that it is most unfair where a farmer has bought a $10,000 herd sire, only to find later that the herd sire reacts to a tuberculosis or brucellosis test, to pay that farmer only $140 in compensation for the herd sire, plus anything he may get for the carcass for bologna purposes, provided the carcass is not condemned. That is quite wrong and is one feature of the entire compensation program that is completely out of line.
Under similar circumstances, if the farmer were unfortunate enough to have his whole herd condemned for foot and mouth disease or some of the other diseases for which whole herds can be condemned, he would get back his full $10,000 that he paid for the herd sire, plus the full value of every one of his animals in the herd.
Coming down to the grade level of cattle, sometimes known as the cross bred level, where there are no certificates of pure breeding, today a cow in full milk in a good dairy herd is worth approximately $300. If this cow should react to a tuberculosis test the owner would receive in compensation $70, plus the salvage value of the cow's carcass for meat, again provided the carcass is not condemned.
If the carcass is fit for meat it will carry a value today of approximately $175 to $200-say, $180. So the farmer gets the compensation of $70 and the salvage value of this cow, if she is otherwise healthy and in good flesh conditon. He gets $180. The man therefore would receive for his $300 cow approximately $250 and would be put to all the trouble of replacing the cow, getting her to market and having her processed. Also he has to undergo the nuisance of having the cow taken from him compulsorily.
Ordinarily, when land is expropriated an extra amount is paid over and above the value of the land, which is compulsorily taken, and that extra amount is for the nuisance of expropriation. Cattlemen who have their
Agriculture
cattle taken from them compulsorily should be given equal consideration.
So much for the milk cow. What about the beef man? What could happen to him under present scales of values? If you went down to Toronto and bought a stocker steer for feeding and finishing, you would find that your ideal stocker steer would weigh around 700 pounds and is worth today around 28 cents per pound. You would pay around $200 for your stocker steer plus the expense of getting him from Toronto to the farmer's location -trucking expenses, and so on. Suppose that in a week or two your stocker steer should react under a tuberculosis test? The owner would get $70 in compensation, and that would be the maximum he could get. The salvage value of that steer is not the original price because, if you remember, originally that steer was worth 28 cents per pound. But as a condemned steer having to go to market and be killed, that stocker steer would go as a common steer at about 17 cents a pound, and so the farmer would get about $119 for his stocker steer, which originally had cost him over $200.
